themes.theme: Documentation and evidence for auditors and reviewers
themes.definition: Duties to keep records and documentation so that an AI project can later be audited, reviewed or explained, including who was responsible, what was decided and on what evidence.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK099 says project teams 'should keep clear records to show how your data or AI system was designed, developed and used, who made a decision and the evidence they used', and 'must' record who is responsible for each part of the system, including suppliers, so that it 'can be audited or reviewed'; it also asks for 'robust reporting mechanisms' for process-based transparency. UK174 recommends 'robust reporting and documentation protocols', traceability across the life cycle, 'evaluation and auditing structures, tracking data provenance, design decisions, training scenarios and processes', and being able to provide evidence that a system 'is operating as expected'. UK268 puts the burden on the audited body: it must 'provide extensive documentation that proves compliance' even for bought-in systems whose code it cannot see, document the work of consultants, show how it handled intellectual property, data protection and ethics, and have the project leader able to supply management documents. UK010 asks energy-sector stakeholders for 'an appropriate audit trail' showing they checked AI use against competition law, and for recordkeeping including board minutes. UK071 checks that 'traceability records, audit trails, documentation like model cards or algorithmic transparency records' exist; AI_Insights wants an internal inventory of user-built agents and access logs showing how access to shared drives is governed. Content is listed, but no retention period, format or named recipient is set.
themes.holders: Project teams and organisations; the auditee and its project leader (UK268); energy-sector stakeholders (UK010); administrators of agent inventories (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: 'Should' throughout, with 'must' for the responsibility record in UK099 (non-statutory guidance) and 'remains their responsibility' in UK268 (good practice). Consequence: not stated.
themes.checks: Mostly records that support checks rather than checks. Where a check is named: UK010's audit trail records that AI use was checked against competition law (trigger not stated; who: stakeholders); UK071 verifies that traceability records exist at the lifecycle stages in its quality-attribute table. What happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: Logs and audit trails of AI outputs, versions and actions taken on AI judgements
themes.definition: Records kept at the level of individual outputs, model versions, threshold settings or actions taken on the basis of an AI judgement, so that particular outputs can later be traced, justified or investigated.
themes.what_is_set_out: AI_Insights says logged generative-AI information (inputs and outputs, per the coder note) should be auditable 'in production' so teams can 'monitor and maintain performance and investigate anomalies'; each bias threshold decision 'should be documented with a clear rationale, including the trade-offs considered and the stakeholders who approved the final values'; gate configuration should be 'version-controlled alongside the model code'; and a 'Complete audit trail' is listed at Critical risk. For AI used to sort and delete government records, AI_Insights wants 'an audit trail of any disposition actions taken on the basis of an AI judgement', a report of records destroyed with 'documentation of the authorisation', a justification for each disposal, an 'AI generated summary of the drives that you dispose of', documentation of how AI was used (possibly in an ATRS report), and a record of 'the tests you conducted against the benchmarks' to explain the choice of tool to the organisation. UK071 asks teams to capture, for each model version, 'who approved it, what test results it passed, what data was used', to archive past versions with version tags (coder note), and to 'Consider storing output logs where needed for future FOI, audits, or investigations'. These are the passages in the cell closest to tracing individual AI outputs after the fact, and they come only from the two technical guidance sources (AI_Insights, UK071); the policy, strategy and audit documents in this cell do not ask for output logs. Retention periods, who reviews the logs, and whether prompts and model settings are logged (beyond threshold configuration) are not stated.
themes.holders: Project, delivery and knowledge and information management (KIM) teams ('you'); otherwise not stated.
themes.binding: Recommended ('should', 'it's important', 'consider', 'might'); the Critical-risk audit trail is labelled 'required' in a non-binding guidance table. Consequence: not stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: ongoing in production (AI_Insights logs); at each model version release (UK071); at each disposal action (AI_Insights); when thresholds are set (AI_Insights). Compared against: benchmarks (AI_Insights records work); test results (UK071); thresholds set by the organisation. Metric or threshold: not stated; the thresholds themselves are to be documented, not given. Who: project or KIM teams; reviewer of the logs not named. What happens with the result: the record is used to 'explain and defend' decisions to the organisation, FOI requesters, auditors and investigators. Model versions: recorded and archived (UK071). Prompts: not stated. Configuration: gate configuration version-controlled (AI_Insights). Confidence scores: not stated.

themes.definition: The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) as a publication and registration duty: which bodies and which tools must have a published record, and for whom it is only recommended or voluntary.
themes.what_is_set_out: The documents agree on a two-level scope but word it differently. UK174 says all central government departments and 'certain arm's length bodies' in scope 'must use it', and that it 'is not a requirement for all arm's length bodies and other public sector institutions yet'; UK099 names departments and arm's length bodies 'that provide public or frontline services, or routinely interact with the general public' and recommends ATRS to local government; UK086 says it is 'mandatory for all government departments, and for ALBs which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public' and recommended 'across the entire public sector'; UK085 says in-scope organisations 'are required to publish ATRS records for algorithmic tools they are currently using in relevant use cases', that publication before Beta or Pilot is voluntary, that out-of-scope tools can still be published, and that transparency 'should be our default position'. DWP's own policy sets a tool-level trigger: AI tools 'must be logged' on ATRS where they have 'a significant influence on a decision-making process which effects the public' or 'directly interact with the general public', with an exemption process (UK190). AI_Insights tells records teams to 'Be prepared to use' ATRS for AI-assisted disposal and to define an ATRS approach before starting; UK071 has 'ATRS transparency record published (yes)' only as an example checklist item. UK085 expects commercial suppliers 'to be comfortable with this level of transparency'. No passage states a sanction, or any monitoring of compliance, for failing to publish.
themes.holders: Central government departments and in-scope arm's length bodies (mandatory); other public sector bodies including local government (recommended); DWP users for DWP tools; responsible teams; commercial suppliers (expected to accept the transparency).
themes.binding: Mandatory by policy for the named central-government group (not statutory); recommended or voluntary for the rest of the public sector; DWP 'must' for its own tools. Consequence of not publishing: not stated anywhere in the cell.
themes.checks: n/a (the ATRS team's review is of the record, not of the tool; see next theme).

themes.theme: ATRS: what a record discloses, how it is cleared, and what may be withheld
themes.definition: The content the ATRS template and guidance ask public bodies to publish about a tool, the review and clearance a record goes through, and the limits on what must be disclosed.
themes.what_is_set_out: A record has a Tier 1 'aimed at the general public', in clear non-technical language with all fields completed and a team (not personal) contact email (UK087, UK086). Tier 2 asks for the responsible organisation and the SRO's role title; the supplier relationships, 'detailing which organisation was or is responsible for which part'; purpose, scope and 'limitations or context where it does not apply'; what the tool replaced; 'the degree of automation'; whether the outputs of the tool and of the wider process 'can be challenged or appealed' (a field that 'must' be completed where UK GDPR Article 22 applies); model type and API provider; 'any bias and fairness evaluation you have undertaken'; any sensitive data processed; and impact assessments with their findings (UK086, UK087). Several limits apply: for off-the-shelf models the organisation has not trained, validated, tested or refined, such as web-based LLMs, the model and development-data sections are left blank; network architecture is withheld for security; whole fields may be marked exempt with a stated reason (UK085); and UK010 separately says transparency 'does not necessarily require disclosure of proprietary code or datasets'. Records are reviewed by the ATRS team, cleared by the operating team, the SRO and the communications team (and a minister in high-profile cases), re-cleared when updated, and marked 'Retired' when a tool is withdrawn (UK086, UK087, UK085). The record asks bodies to describe checks and appeal routes, not to have them: bias evaluation is reported 'you have undertaken', and an appeals process only 'If so' (N/A allowed).
themes.holders: The organisation, department or public sector body completing the record and its responsible team; the SRO; the communications or press team; ministers (high-profile cases); the ATRS team as reviewer.
themes.binding: Required fields for organisations in mandatory scope (policy, not statute); many content items are 'should' or 'should aim'; the Article 22 appeals field is 'must'. Consequence: not stated, except that the coder note infers the ATRS team will not publish without clearance.
themes.checks: This theme concerns disclosure of checks, not the checks themselves. Bias and fairness evaluation: disclosed if done (performance over subgroups; the coder note lists precision, recall and F1 as suggested metrics); no requirement to test and no threshold. Human involvement: the 'degree of automation' and how humans are involved are described, not required. Appeals: described if any. Trigger for updating the record: substantive change, and retirement. Who: the completing organisation; the ATRS team reviews the record. What happens with the result: publication on GOV.UK. Off-the-shelf LLMs: no model specification is disclosed, so model identity and version for such tools are not in the record. Prompts, model versions and confidence scores: not stated.

quotes.quote: For off-the-shelf models that your organisation has not trained, validated, tested, or applied any refinement techniques to (e.g. Web UI-based LLMs), please leave both the Model Specification (2.4.2) and following Development Data Specification (2.4.3) sections blank
You should also describe any bias and fairness evaluation you have undertaken (i.e. model performance over subgroups within the dataset), and any measures taken to address issues you identify.
Can a member of the public appeal the decisions assisted by the tool? If so, state the appeals process.
Transparency does not necessarily require disclosure of proprietary code or datasets, which may be too complex or protected by intellectual property rights.

themes.theme: Other publication: assessments, evaluation results, code, data and governance information
themes.definition: Recommendations or commitments to make information about AI projects public outside the ATRS: impact assessments, evaluation and pilot results, source code and data, explanations of how a system works, and organisations' own AI approach.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK099 calls publishing the DPIA and the equality impact assessment 'good practice', recommends making project information public (GitHub, blogs, GOV.UK), publishing source code 'if possible', open data with a DOI where data are non-sensitive and supplier agreements allow, and publishing how the system works and how life-cycle decisions made it 'ethical, lawful and trustworthy'; UK216 includes publishing equality assessment results as a checklist step; UK268 puts 'publication of relevant information' in release criteria; AI_Insights 'strongly recommend[s] coding in the open' and UK136 asks for 'working in the open where possible'. On evaluation, UK082 recommends pilots with 'robust evaluation and publishing results'; UK133 asks evaluators to be open about the limits of generalising and to 'specify which AI model was used in the intervention and how it was used', and presents evaluation as one way to 'ensure the Government is accountable to the public', though the coder note records that it does not require publication. UK206 lists 'External transparency and reporting processes' and public communication of assurance steps; UK174 lists 'public transparency' about a department's AI use. The NAO commits to publish its own AI risk, assurance and decision artefacts and to report its AI use in its Transparency Report. Nearly all of this is optional. There is a tension between the encouragement to publish code (UK099, AI_Insights, UK136) and UK010's view that transparency need not extend to proprietary code (with UK086's intellectual-property caveat).
themes.holders: Project teams and public organisations; evaluators (UK133); public bodies carrying out equality assessments (UK216); the NAO for its own AI use.
themes.binding: 'Good practice', 'should consider', 'if possible', 'strongly recommend', 'might include'; NAO commitments are 'will'. UK082 recommendations had no recorded acceptance in the coded text. Consequence: not stated.
themes.checks: n/a. One item bears on checking outputs: evaluation reports should name 'which AI model was used ... and how it was used' (UK133), which ties findings to a model; model version and configuration are not mentioned.

themes.theme: Telling people that AI is in use
themes.definition: Duties or recommendations to tell the public, service users or data subjects that AI is being used, that content was produced by AI, or how their data is processed.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 asks that automated responses be labelled (a chatbot reply should say something like 'this response has been written by an automated AI chatbot'), says organisations 'must ensure that they are aware of the presence of the AI system' so that people can contest it, and that facial recognition in public areas 'need[s]' clear signage. UK268 lists 'Inform users when they are interacting with AI' and disclosure of synthetic content as expected controls; UK099 asks for disclosure 'when AI has been used to produce an output', for internal as well as external uses, and for privacy notices that include how to complain; UK010 asks energy-sector stakeholders to communicate 'that AI is being used, the purpose of its use' and to give privacy information. DWP requires staff to 'declare the use of AI tools for official business if requested', for example under a Freedom of Information or subject access request (UK190). UK139 asks regulators to encourage developers and deployers 'to notify end users when they are affected by or engaging with an AI system'. Strength runs from restated statute (privacy information) and DWP's policy 'must', through 'must' in non-statutory guidance (UK174), to 'should' and 'consider'. Several documents link notice directly to challenge: people cannot contest what they do not know is there (UK174, UK139).
themes.holders: Public organisations and project teams; data controllers; DWP users (on request); energy-sector stakeholders (UK010); developers and deployers, encouraged by regulators (UK139).
themes.binding: Statutory where it restates UK GDPR privacy information; 'must' by policy in DWP; 'must' or 'need to' in non-statutory guidance (UK174); otherwise 'should', 'expected control' or 'consider'. Consequence of not disclosing: not stated.

themes.definition: Duties or recommendations to explain how an AI system works, or how a particular output or decision was reached, to affected people, users, regulators or those overseeing the system.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 restates the UK GDPR duty to give 'meaningful information about the logic involved' in automated decision-making, asks organisations to consider transparency before deploying, and recommends individual-level explanations 'where this is requested'; UK099 repeats the on-request individual explanation. UK268 says explainability 'should be proportionate to the risk' and depends on the audience 'such as a regulator or member of the public', asks organisations to 'Justify the use of black-box models', and restates that citizens have a right to understand decisions 'supported or made by AI systems'. UK010 asks for 'an appropriate level of explanation of the AI they use', for explanations of forecasting methods and black-box outputs, and states a 'duty to be transparent about adjustments' in grid management, with AI influence explainable 'in a manner that is proportionate to the risk'. UK071's explainability module aims for decisions that 'can be understood, traced, and explained' by overseers and by affected people; the NAO commits to use AI 'in ways that are explainable, so that outputs can be understood, tested and challenged where necessary'. UK136 tells buyers to 'Avoid relying on black-box algorithms' and to require an explainable approach in tenders, though its stated reason (coder note) is internal understanding and avoiding supplier lock-in rather than explanation to the public. Explanation is usually owed 'on request' or 'proportionately', and no document sets a standard for what an adequate explanation of a given output contains.
themes.holders: Data controllers; public organisations and project teams; energy-sector stakeholders and organisations processing data with AI (UK010); the NAO for its own AI; central government buyers and, through tenders, suppliers (UK136); developers and deployers, encouraged by regulators (UK139).
themes.binding: Statutory where restating UK GDPR on automated decision-making; 'duty' in UK010 for grid adjustments (source of duty not cited in the passage); 'must consider' in UK174; otherwise 'should', 'consider' or organisational principle. Consequence: UK268 names the risk of 'Insufficient information for end-users to challenge or appeal outcomes'; otherwise not stated.
themes.checks: Mostly n/a. UK071 treats explainability as something to test (the coder note gives a simulated 'Why was I rejected?' query); trigger, comparator, metric, who and what happens with the result: not stated. UK268: the required level of explanation is 'proportionate to the risk', with no metric. The NAO principle links explanation to outputs being 'tested and challenged', without saying how.

themes.theme: Acknowledging limitations, uncertainty and residual risk
themes.definition: Requirements to state openly what an AI system or its data cannot do, that its outputs are uncertain, and which risks remain after mitigation.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 says organisations 'need to make it explicit that the outputs of your AI systems are statistically informed guesses rather than facts', including the data source and how the inference was generated. UK099 asks teams to 'Disclose any limitations of the data, such as quality issues, missing or incomplete data, gaps in representativeness, or known errors'. UK268 says that where 'fairness cannot be fully assured, risks should be transparently acknowledged and managed'. UK071 says residual risks and ethical concerns 'must be formally acknowledged' and that a remaining bias disparity 'should be consciously signed-off with rationale'. UK133 asks evaluators to be open about the limits on carrying evaluation findings over to new policies, and the ATRS asks for a tool's scope and 'limitations or context where it does not apply' (UK086). The audience differs: affected people or users [inference] in UK174, the public in ATRS, internal sign-off in UK071, and is not stated in UK268. No consequence is stated for failing to disclose.
themes.holders: Public organisations and project teams; evaluators (UK133); organisations completing ATRS records; in UK071 and UK268 the holder is not stated.
themes.binding: 'Need to' in non-statutory guidance (UK174); 'must' within a non-mandatory framework (UK071); otherwise 'should' or imperative guidance. Consequence: not stated.
themes.checks: Bears on checking outputs. UK174 treats every output as an uncertain inference that must be presented as such. UK071 gives an example acceptance criterion, 'Residual risks: Documented and accepted or mitigated (none critical outstanding)' (coder note). Trigger: user acceptance stage before deployment (UK071); otherwise not stated. Compared against: not stated. Who: not stated. What happens with the result: formal acknowledgement or sign-off with rationale (UK071).

themes.definition: Mechanisms through which people affected by an AI-supported decision can challenge it, complain, ask for review or correction, or obtain redress, including data-subject rights used for the same purpose.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 is the strongest in wording: organisations 'must establish and promote clear and accessible mechanisms for people to challenge the decisions made by AI systems', designed 'before deployment' and maintained for the system's life, and 'need to establish recourse and feedback mechanisms' for harm or errors. UK099 says teams 'must' provide 'routes for people to raise concerns, complaints or request corrections' and 'should' handle 'feedback, complaints and appeals', and describes redress as asking 'for the decision to be reviewed or corrected, especially in the case of automated decision making'. UK268 lists challenge, appeal and redress as an expected control; UK206 asks that appeals be 'simple and – importantly – effective'; UK010 asks only that redress be considered within governance and offered to consumers treated unfairly. UK139 asks regulators to make clear 'which existing routes to contestability apply', describes a chain in which users contest with deployers and deployers with developers, and says contestability is 'ultimately the responsibility of AI developers and deployers'. Data-subject rights (access, correction, objection, withdrawing consent, erasure) are restated as routes (UK174, UK099, UK010). Against this, AI_Insights requires a 'User appeal mechanism' only at Critical risk and names 'contestability and redress' only as a theme to consider, and the ATRS asks only whether an appeal exists ('If so'). No passage names who hears an appeal, sets a timescale, or defines the remedy.
themes.holders: Public organisations and project teams; data controllers; energy-sector stakeholders (UK010); AI developers and deployers, with regulators promoting the practice (UK139); the operator of the application (AI_Insights); organisations completing ATRS records.
themes.binding: 'Must' in non-statutory guidance (UK174, UK099); statutory where data-subject rights are restated; 'should', 'expected control' or 'can include' elsewhere; required only at Critical risk in AI_Insights; disclosure-only in ATRS. Consequence of having no route: not stated.
themes.checks: A challenge is a trigger for human review of a decision, not a check in itself. Trigger: a person's challenge, complaint or request, after the decision. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who reviews: not stated (UK174's SROs monitor reports; see the next theme). What happens with the result: review or correction of the decision (UK099); 'any required redress from harms' (UK268); otherwise not stated.
